transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I just... I really didn't know where else to go because things are just getting so out of hand. What brings me in is, well, I work down at the dry cleaners—I've been doing laundry and dry cleaning work for years—and lately I just cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. 

I mean, it used to be that I could at least sort of juggle it, but now? It's a complete disaster area. I'll have the little claim tickets from the morning drop-offs, and then the register receipts, and then all my workshop notes about which garments need special spot treatments or what the seamstress needs to fix... and then the actual customer jobs themselves, the clothes and the bags. It all just ends up piled together in this huge, overwhelming mountain on the counter or in the back room. I try to sort it out, I really do try to make piles, but they just merge together into one big mess, and I'll stand there staring at it all until I honestly do not know what to handle first. It's like my brain just completely short-circuits looking at the clutter, and I get so upset because I just stand there, completely frozen, trying to figure out where to even begin with it all.
Looking back to when you were in school or growing up, did you have similar difficulties with organization, staying focused, or keeping track of your things?

Oh, gosh, yes. It’s funny you ask that because I was just thinking about my old desk in the third or fourth grade. You know those old wooden ones with the little cubby hole underneath where you’re supposed to keep your textbooks and your pencil case? Mine was just crammed full of crumpled-up worksheets and broken crayons and permission slips I was supposed to take home but never did. 

Even way back then, in grade school, it was always the exact same story. My teachers—I remember Mrs. Gable specifically, she had this perfectly organized classroom—she would always pull my mother aside at those parent-teacher conferences. And she’d tell her, you know, she’d say that I was a very bright girl, that I had a lot of potential, but I was just so scattered. That was the word they always used, "scattered." Because I was always blurting things out, just talking completely out of turn before anyone even called on me, and I was constantly losing my papers. I mean, my homework would just vanish into thin air between my kitchen table and the classroom. 

And they were always having to stand over my shoulder and give me these constant reminders just to finish my work. I’d start a spelling test or a math sheet, and then I’d be looking out the window at a bird, or turning around to talk to the kid behind me, and the teacher would have to tap on my desk and say, "Focus, back to your paper." It was exhausting for my poor mother, honestly, having to hear the same thing every single year. She tried getting me those big binders with the color-coded folders to help me, but I’d just shove everything into the front pocket anyway until the plastic ripped. It just... it never really got better, no matter how hard I tried to keep it all straight. It's just like the dry cleaning tickets now, just a different kind of paper I can't keep track of.
In your everyday adult life, do you often feel restless inside, like you always need to be moving or are driven by a motor?

Restless? I... well, I don't know if I'd say I feel like I'm driven by a motor, exactly. I mean, my husband, he's always telling me I can't just sit still and watch a movie, because I'm always getting up to check on the laundry or wipe down the counters, but I don't really feel this... this inner buzzing or anything like that. 

I know some people talk about feeling like they just have to run a marathon or they're going to explode out of their skin, but for me, it's not really like that. I'm on my feet all day at the dry cleaners anyway, hauling heavy bags of clothes and moving back and forth between the front counter and the pressing machines, so by the time I get home, my feet are just aching. I'm pretty tired physically. I might fidget a bit with my hands—like, I'll twist my rings around or I'll catch myself peeling the label off a water bottle while I'm watching TV—but I don't feel that intense, constant need to just be on the go all the time. 

I mean, I'm not running around the house doing jumping jacks or anything. It's more just... my mind is what's always going a mile a minute, you know? But my body? I wouldn't say I feel restless inside like a motor. I just feel like a tired 54-year-old woman who's been standing on hard linoleum for eight hours. So, no, I don't think I really have that specific feeling you're talking about.
In your daily conversations, do you often find yourself interrupting other people while they are talking?

Oh, interrupting... yes. Yes, I do that a lot, actually. It's... it's a terrible habit, and I feel so guilty about it because I know how it looks, but I just can't seem to stop myself. 

At the dry cleaners, for example, I have a couple of younger girls who work for me, helping out on the floor and sorting the incoming orders. And they'll be standing there, talking to each other about, you know, whatever it is they talk about—their weekend plans, or a customer who just came in, or they'll be trying to figure out which bin a silk blouse is supposed to go into. And I’ll be walking by, or even just standing at the register, and before I even realize what my mouth is doing, I'm just cutting right into their conversation. I'll just blurt out an answer to a question they weren't even asking me, or I'll finish their sentence for them because they're taking too long to get to the point and my brain has already jumped ahead to what they're going to say. 

And it's not just talking, either! It's physical things, too. Like, I'll see one of the girls sorting a pile of clothes, and maybe she's putting the wool sweaters a little too close to the delicate silks, which you really shouldn't do because the fibers can transfer, and instead of just waiting or gently saying something, I'll just reach right over her shoulder and start moving the clothes myself. I just jump right in and take over before they even have a chance to ask for my help or realize what they're doing. 

I know it comes off like I'm butting in, or like I'm this overbearing boss who has to micromanage everything. I can see it on their faces, you know? They get that tight little smile and they step back, and I think, "Oh, I did it again." I really don't mean to be rude, I just... it's like the impulse is so strong. I see something that needs fixing, or I hear a conversation where I know the answer, and I just have to insert myself into it right that second. I can't just hold it in and wait my turn. It's exactly like when I was a little girl blurting out answers in Mrs. Gable's class, honestly. I just... I haven't grown out of it. It's very frustrating, especially when I'm trying to maintain a good relationship with my staff, because nobody likes to be constantly interrupted or corrected like that.
Do you often find that you talk excessively, or have people close to you commented that you talk too much?

Oh, Lord, yes. My husband would probably laugh out loud if he heard you ask that. It’s... well, it's something I’ve always done, but it really gets away from me. Once I get going on a topic, it’s like a train going downhill without brakes. 

Take the shop, for instance. A customer will come in with, say, a tough stain on a nice garment—maybe a red wine spill on a silk blouse, or grease on a wool suit lapel. And they’ll just ask a simple question, like, "Can you get this out?" But instead of just saying yes or no, I launch into this whole... presentation. Once I start explaining a cleaning method to a customer, I just can't seem to stop myself. I’ll go into all the details about how we have to use a specific enzyme spot-treatment before it goes into the machine, and how the solvent works differently on natural fibers compared to synthetics, and how we have to adjust the steam pressure on the press so we don't shine the fabric... 

And the whole time, I can actually hear myself going on and on. It’s like a part of my brain is floating above me saying, "Okay, that’s enough, let the poor man leave," but my mouth just keeps moving! I can see them literally edging toward the door, clutching their ticket, shifting their weight from one foot to the other, trying to politely nod their way out of the conversation, and I just keep talking at them.

And it’s not just at the dry cleaners, either. It happens at church all the time. Like after choir practice on Thursday nights. We usually mingle a bit in the fellowship hall before heading home, and I'll start talking to one of the other altos about the hymns we're practicing, or maybe just about the church potluck. And before I know it, I'm giving them a twenty-minute monologue about my grandmother's potato salad recipe and how the grocery store was out of the right kind of paprika, and then how the price of eggs has gone up. I’ll be following them out into the hallway, still talking, even when they’ve got their coat on and their keys in their hand, clearly trying to escape to the parking lot. 

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I know I'm holding people hostage with my talking. I hear myself doing it, I see them edging away, but the words just keep tumbling out anyway. I just have so much to say and it all feels so important in the moment, you know?

When people are speaking directly to me? Oh... well, yes. That... that actually does happen. I hate to admit it, but yes, it really does. 

My helper at the front counter—her name is Sarah, sweet girl, she's been with me for about two years now since she got out of high school—she will be standing right in front of me, I mean literally two feet away across the sorting bin. And she’ll be telling me a customer's specific instructions. You know, like Mr. Henderson dropped off his button-downs and he wants heavy starch, or maybe Mrs. Davis brought in her husband's linen shirts and wants absolutely no starch because it makes the natural fibers too brittle. 

And I will look right at Sarah. I’ll look her dead in the eye, and I nod my head, and I'll even say, "Uh-huh, got it." I look like I am hanging on her every word, like I'm completely dialed in to the conversation. But then... I don't even know where my mind goes, to be honest with you. It’s like I hear the sound of her voice, but the actual words just bounce right off my forehead. 

Because I kid you not, less than a minute later, I'll be holding that exact same shirt, getting ready to pin the tag on it for the laundry side, and I have to turn right back around and say, "Wait, Sarah, what did you just say? Was it starch or no starch?" 

And she just looks at me like I have two heads! Because I *just* agreed with her! I just nodded at her not sixty seconds prior. It makes me feel terrible, it really does, because I don't want her—or anyone else, for that matter—to think I don't care about what they're saying. I do care! Getting the starch preference right is incredibly important in this business. If you put heavy starch on a shirt that's supposed to be soft, the customer comes back furious, and rightfully so, because the collar will chafe their neck all day. But no matter how hard I try to lock onto the words when someone is standing right there talking directly to my face, my brain just... takes a little vacation, I guess. I'll be thinking about the spotting board or if we have enough hangers, and the actual conversation I'm having just completely evaporates.

Do I often have trouble finishing things I'm told to do? Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I do. It’s... well, it’s a real problem for me, especially if there’s a sequence to it. 

Like, if someone gives me three things to do all at once. Let's say my manager comes out from the back and says, "Okay, before noon, I need you to call the supplier, tag that silk blouse, and enter the receipt." And I will hear every single word. I'll nod my head and say, "Absolutely, I'm on it." 

And I always start off so strong! I will go right over to the phone by the register and call the supplier. We use a distributor a few towns over for our wire hangers and poly bags, and you have to talk to this fellow named Dave to make sure it gets on the afternoon truck, so I will get that all sorted out right then and there. I do that first thing perfectly. But the second I hang up that phone... it is like the rest of the instructions just fall right out of my ear. 

I'll turn around to go deal with the silk blouse—because you know, silk is so incredibly delicate, you really have to be careful where you place the tag, usually on the care label, so you don't puncture a visible thread and ruin the garment—and on my way over to the counter, I'll get completely pulled into something else. I'll see a pile of heavy wool coats that need to be moved to the conveyor, or I'll notice the lint trap on the big commercial dryer needs emptying, and I just start doing that instead. 

And then two hours will go by, and my manager will come back out to the front and ask if the receipt is entered in the computer system yet. And I'll just freeze. Because the silk blouse is still sitting there completely untagged, the receipt is just crumpled up in the bottom of my apron pocket, and I'm standing there halfway through emptying a lint trap. I usually do the very first thing I'm told, but I almost always get pulled into something else before the rest of the list is finished. It just completely slips my mind once I start moving around the shop.

Avoid things that take a lot of brainpower? Like heavy thinking or paperwork? Oh, no, I wouldn't say I do that. No, not at all. I actually don't mind that kind of work. 

Take the end-of-the-month inventory and the supply ordering, for instance. That is a massive job that takes a whole lot of concentration. We have to count every single box of wire hangers—and they come in boxes of 500, mind you. Plus, you have to separate them out because we have the 18-inch suit hangers, the 16-inch standard shirt hangers, and then the special ones with the little textured cardboard tubes on the bottom for trousers so the fabric doesn't get that awful permanent crease in the middle of the leg. 

And then there's the chemicals and the solvents. We use a hydrocarbon solvent now, not the old perc, because the environmental regulations changed back in—oh, when was it, maybe 2010 or 2011? My father had an absolute fit about the cost of upgrading the dry cleaning machines, I mean he was just beside himself, but it really is so much better for the environment and it doesn't have that harsh chemical smell.
